The Sacred Bow: Warfare, Medicine & Defense in Anaguta Heritage

By Elder Bitrus Azi & Tradomodern Heritage Lab

For centuries, the rugged highlands of Jos North formed an unassailable fortress for the Anaguta people. But rock and ravine alone did not secure their freedom — at the heart of Anaguta survival was an instrument of immense reverence: the Tukwi, the sacred hunting and war bow.

The Anatomy of the Tukwi

Unlike standard plains bows, the Anaguta bow was carved exclusively from slow-growth mountain acacia wood, cured over smoldering hearth embers to maximize tensile elasticity. Bowstrings were fashioned from twisted antelope sinew or cured wild hemp cordage, capable of withstanding the harsh harmattan winds of the Jos plateau.

Archers were trained from childhood, not solely in marksmanship, but in herbal botany. The tips of war arrows were dipped in secret botanical mixtures known only to master hunters. In tactical skirmishes, Anaguta warriors utilized natural granite caves and watchtowers to spot approaching invaders leagues away, deploying whistling signaling arrows that coordinated defense across clan compounds.

Honor and Cultural Ethos

The bow was never regarded merely as a weapon of violence; it was an emblem of manhood, responsibility, and defensive honor. To draw the Tukwi unjustly was considered an offense against the ancestors. When a warrior passed into the ancestral realm, his personal bow was hung within the ancestral shrine, symbolizing unbroken vigilance over his descendants.

"Our ancestors never waged wars of territorial conquest. The bow was forged to safeguard our hearths, our children, and the sacred granaries nested inside Naraguta's rock caverns."
— Anaguta Council of Elders Archival Oral History

Preservation for the Modern Generation

Today, as modern sports and digital entertainment capture youth attention, the Anaguta Tradomodern initiative hosts annual archery workshops during the Ishokori festival, ensuring that every young Anaguta can hold the seasoned wood, string the sinew cord, and remember the courage that preserved their freedom.
